historical_timeline.summary: Elected to a studentship at Christ Church, Oxford; BA 1656; medical studies follow.
His father dies, of consumption or a kindred malady by his biographer's account; his brother dies of consumption soon after.
Physician in Lord Ashley's household; friendship with Sydenham; the abscess operation of June 1668.
A cough begins that troubles him for the rest of his life.
Bachelor of Medicine (February 1674/5); in France, mostly at Montpellier, from late 1675 to 1677.
Back in London, he must leave the city often, and always in winter, because of its coal smoke.
Political exile in Holland; returns in February 1689.
Settles at Oates, High Laver, Essex.
Writes that his lungs cannot bear the smoke of the city.
Visits Cambridge at a friend's invitation.
Back at Oates after a day in London left him hardly able to breathe.
Board of Trade: in London only in the warmer months.
Breathless lying flat during a winter visit to London.
Sore legs keep him in bed; deafness for a time.
Dies at Oates, aged 72, after a year of increasing breathlessness and leg swelling.
Biographers and historians describe his illness as a lifelong cough, possible consumption, and asthma.

claims.statement: John Locke was born on 29 August 1632 (Julian; 8 September 1632, Gregorian) at Wrington, Somerset, to Puritan parents of modest means. His father, John Locke (1606 to 1661), was a country attorney who served in a cavalry company on the Parliamentary side early in the Civil War; his mother was Agnes Keene. He had one brother, Thomas, born in 1637.
He was educated at Westminster School and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he was elected to a studentship in 1652 and took his BA in 1656.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Westminster entry is dated 1646 in one source and 1647 in another; the record gives no year.

claims.statement: His father died on 13 February 1660/1 (Julian), at about 54, of consumption or some kindred malady, by his biographer's account; his only brother, Thomas, died of consumption soon afterwards, at about 26, leaving no children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A nineteenth-century biographer's account; 'consumption' then meant a wasting chest disease, usually but not always tuberculosis.

claims.statement: He studied medicine at Oxford and took the degree of Bachelor of Medicine in February 1674/5, with a licence to practise, but never took the doctorate. From 1667 he lived in the household of Lord Ashley (later the first Earl of Shaftesbury) as his physician, and in June 1668 he organized the surgical drainage of a large abscess above Ashley's liver, with advice from leading physicians including Thomas Sydenham.
claims.clinical_interpretation: DNB dates the degree to 1674 and Williams to 6 February 1675; under the English year that began on 25 March these are the same day.

claims.statement: From about 1667 he was a close friend of the physician Thomas Sydenham, accompanied him on visits to patients, helped him with his writings, and was praised by him; Sydenham embraced careful observation of disease.

His biographer H. R. Fox Bourne wrote that about 1670 Locke began to have a cough that seriously troubled him through the remainder of his life, and that an undated fragment in his hand from those years, titled 'Tussis', was the start of a paper on coughs. His health was already weak by the early 1670s; a letter from Sydenham, probably at the end of 1674, advised him to go to bed early and be very temperate and cautious, and from late 1675 to 1677 he lived in France, mostly at Montpellier, then much visited by invalids.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The onset of a lifelong cough in his late thirties is documented; its cause is not.

claims.statement: Lady Masham later wrote that although his travels in France had done his health some good, after his return he was still less able than before to stay long in London without retreating to a neighbouring village 'to recover the prejudice his health received from the smoke of that vast quantity of sea-coal which is burnt in this great city'. From then on he left London as often as he could, and always in the winter months.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A close friend's account, written after his death, linking his illness to London's coal smoke.

source_links.locator: Vol. 1, chapter 8, quoting Lady Masham to Le Clerc, 12 January 1704/5

claims.statement: Among his medical papers, an account of consumption that Fox Bourne describes as drawn from Sydenham's observation and confirmed by Locke attributes the frequency of consumptions in London to 'a perpetual mist' mixed with the fumes of the city's trades, 'but especially the sulphur and fumes of sea coals, with which the air is repleted; and these being sucked into our lungs ... give an occasion to a cough'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Seventeenth-century medical theory, recorded as such; it shows that he and Sydenham linked coal smoke with cough.

source_links.locator: Vol. 1, chapter 8, 'Extracts of Sydenham's Physic Books'

claims.statement: He left England in the autumn of 1683, when he was under suspicion for his association with Shaftesbury, lived in Holland, and landed at Greenwich on 12 February 1688/9 (Julian). He soon declined a diplomatic mission on the ground of insufficient health, and wrote in April 1689 that he hoped to breathe more easily and be less troubled by his cough.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His exile was political; the sources read do not say that he went to Holland for his health.

source_links.locator: Vol. 2, chapter 10, Locke to Limborch, 12 April 1689

claims.statement: He found the smoke of London unfavourable to his health, and from the spring of 1691 lived at Oates, in the parish of High Laver, Essex, the home of Sir Francis and Lady Masham (Damaris Cudworth).

On 29 February 1691/2 (Julian; 10 March 1692, Gregorian) he wrote to Philipp van Limborch that since visiting Robert Boyle on his deathbed in December, 'my health has kept me in the country, for I found my lungs could not bear the smoke of the city'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own words, in Fox Bourne's translation of the Latin letter.

source_links.locator: Vol. 2, chapter 12, Locke to Limborch, 29 February 1691-2

claims.statement: In May 1692 he spent a day or two at Cambridge after Isaac Newton wrote to him on 3 May (Julian) that, now the churlish weather was almost over, he hoped to see him there.

source_links.locator: Vol. 2, chapter 12, Newton to Locke, 3 May 1692

claims.statement: In November 1692 he wrote that after a single day in London he fell so ill that he could hardly breathe and had to come away; back at Oates on 28 November (Julian) he told Edward Clarke, 'well I cannot say I yet am, under so troublesome a cough as I have, but my lungs move easier than they did'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of breathlessness in London relieved in the country.

source_links.locator: Vol. 2, chapter 12, Locke to Limborch and to Clarke, 28 November 1692

claims.statement: As a commissioner of the Board of Trade from 1696 to 1700 he suffered so much from his chest illness, which the Stanford Encyclopedia calls asthma, that he could bear the smoke of London only in the four warmer months; he attended its meetings in the summer and autumn and was confined to Oates the rest of the year. In October 1698 he wrote that 'a troublesome cough and great difficulty of breathing' were forcing him out of town.

source_links.locator: Vol. 2, chapter 14, Locke to Limborch, 18 October 1698

claims.statement: Summoned to London to see the king on 23 January 1697/8 (Julian), he wrote to Lord Somers that when he lay down in bed his breath failed him, so that he had to sit up most of the night and at three in the morning got up and sat by the fire till morning; he returned to Oates at once, and declined the employment offered because of his health.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own description of breathlessness lying flat during a winter visit to London.

claims.statement: From 1700 he was often kept in bed by sore legs and wrote of 'my old evil of my breast'; by 1702 he had become so deaf for a time that he could hardly take part in conversation.

In June 1704 he wrote that his shortness of breath and uneasiness increased every day, despite the season that usually restored him. That summer his legs swelled, more so towards the end of October. Lady Masham wrote that all the faculties of his mind were perfect to the last, and that he died of weakness alone. On 28 October 1704 (Julian; 8 November 1704, Gregorian), carried to his chair while she read the psalms to him, he died quietly at Oates, aged 72. He was buried in the churchyard at High Laver.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented decline of his last year: increasing breathlessness, leg swelling, and weakness; no cause of death was recorded.

source_links.locator: Vol. 2, chapter 15, Locke to King, 1 June 1704; Le Clerc's eloge; Lady Masham

claims.statement: Modern accounts describe him as asthmatic: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy states that he was asthmatic, and a 2006 history of medicine article that his health was blighted throughout life by asthma, which often incapacitated him for long periods.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective label in modern secondary sources; no physician's diagnosis from his lifetime is recorded.

claims.statement: Fox Bourne judged that his cough was connected with disease in the lungs, and that probably only extreme care in treating himself had kept it from passing into a rapid consumption.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A nineteenth-century biographer's interpretation. No source read diagnoses tuberculosis; his long survival argues against it.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate a 59-year-old never-smoker with a lifelong cough, wheeze, and breathlessness, worse in city air and by open fires at home: pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry interpreted with race-neutral GLI equations and the ATS/ERS 1688 bronchodilator criterion, FeNO, blood eosinophils and IgE, DLCO, alpha-1 antitrypsin, NT-proBNP, an interferon-gamma release assay, chest X-ray, and CT for persistent airflow limitation; a reasoned decision between asthma with persistent airflow limitation and COPD from non-tobacco exposures (GINA 1691, GOLD 1691); GINA track 1 budesonide-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy with add-on tiotropium; inhaler technique, adherence, and a written action plan with peak-flow zones; pulmonary rehabilitation; air pollution as a cause and exposure reduction (WHO 1687 air quality guidelines, air quality alerts, removing indoor solid-fuel smoke, HEPA air cleaning, respirators on unavoidable high-pollution days); vaccinations; and management of a viral flare by the action plan (CMID asthma and COPD monographs).

Alpha-1 antitrypsin is normal, the interferon-gamma release assay is negative, NT-proBNP is normal, and the chest X-ray is clear. COPD from non-tobacco exposures was considered, because GOLD recognizes COPD in never-smokers exposed to air pollution and solid-fuel smoke and his post-bronchodilator ratio is below 0.70. The persistent limitation is best explained by long-standing asthma, with pollution and indoor smoke as aggravating causes. Dr. Nwankwo-Fairfax agrees. Because GINA and GOLD advise that anyone with asthma features be treated as asthma, inhaled corticosteroid is essential and a long-acting bronchodilator alone is not safe

referral.question: A 59-year-old never-smoker with a cough since his late thirties and wheeze and breathlessness, worse every winter, in city air, and by open coal and wood fires at home. Please confirm the diagnosis (asthma, COPD from non-tobacco exposures, or both), advise on CT, and recommend treatment and pulmonary rehabilitation
referral.urgency: Routine, within two to three weeks; he is not in distress and has a reliever
referral.pertinent_history: Mr. Locke is a 59-year-old philosopher and author, trained in medicine, who has never smoked. He has coughed since his late thirties, worse each winter and within a day of any stay in the city, and better in warm weather and country air. For a year he has lodged in a country house where he reads most evenings by an open fire of coal and wood; before that he lived about 30 years in a large city near main roads. This winter he has had night cough two or three times a week, wheeze, and breathlessness after one flight of stairs, and after a recent city trip he could hardly breathe. No hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, orthopnea, ankle swelling, reflux, or rhinitis. His father and brother died of consumption, by family account. Asthma Control Test 12; weight 62.0 kg, height 178 cm; oxygen saturation 95 percent; prolonged expiration with scattered wheeze; no clubbing or crackles. Chest X-ray today shows mild hyperinflation only. I have started albuterol as needed, asked him to stop using the open fires, and ordered a blood count with eosinophils, IgE, alpha-1 antitrypsin, NT-proBNP, and an interferon-gamma release assay. Full lung function tests with bronchodilator response, FeNO, and DLCO are booked at your laboratory on the day of your visit
questions: Does he have asthma, COPD from non-tobacco exposures, or features of both, and how should the airflow limitation be interpreted?
Is a CT of the chest indicated, and what does it show?
How much do outdoor air pollution and indoor solid-fuel smoke contribute, and what exposure reduction do you advise?
What monitoring and follow-up do you advise?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Locke is seen at the request of Dr. Hartwell-Osei. He has had a cough since his late thirties, with wheeze and breathlessness that have grown over the years; symptoms are worst in winter, in cold air, in the city, and by smoky fires, and ease in summer and in the country. He has never smoked or vaped and has had no occupational dust or fume exposure. He lived about 30 years in a large city near main roads and for the past year has lodged in a country house with open coal and wood fires, which have been out of use for two weeks. He has had no hemoptysis, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, nasal symptoms, reflux, or breathlessness lying flat. He has never had an oral corticosteroid course or an emergency visit for breathing. On albuterol as needed he uses one or two doses a day. His father and brother died of consumption
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Spirometry this morning (GLI Global race-neutral equations): FEV1 2.11 L (62 percent predicted) and FVC 3.71 L before bronchodilator, FEV1/FVC 0.57; 15 minutes after albuterol 400 mcg, FEV1 2.49 L (+380 mL, 11 percent of predicted) and FVC 4.02 L, FEV1/FVC 0.62 (lower limit of normal 0.67); DLCO 26.4 mL/min/mmHg (predicted 26.9); FeNO 41 ppb; six-minute walk 430 m with lowest saturation 94 percent. CT of the chest today without contrast, with expiratory images: diffuse bronchial wall thickening and mosaic attenuation with air trapping; no emphysema, bronchiectasis, nodules, or interstitial disease. From the first visit: eosinophils 0.46 x 10^3/uL, IgE 186 IU/mL, alpha-1 antitrypsin 131 mg/dL, NT-proBNP 58 pg/mL, interferon-gamma release assay negative (0.02 IU/mL), and a chest X-ray with mild hyperinflation only. Asthma Control Test 13 today

Regular rhythm; jugular venous pressure not raised; no edema

assessment.display: Asthma with persistent airflow limitation, type 2 phenotype
assessment.assessment: He has airflow limitation that persists after bronchodilator (FEV1/FVC 0.62, below the lower limit of normal and below 0.70) with a large bronchodilator response. GOLD recognizes COPD in never-smokers from air pollution and solid-fuel smoke, so COPD was considered. The weight of evidence is for asthma: onset in his late thirties, symptoms that vary with season, cold, and smoke, a bronchodilator response of 380 mL, FeNO 41 ppb, eosinophils 0.46 x 10^3/uL, a raised IgE, a normal DLCO, and a CT showing airway disease without emphysema. The persistent limitation most likely reflects decades of under-treated asthma with airway remodeling, worsened by pollution and indoor smoke. Treat as asthma: an inhaled corticosteroid is essential, and a long-acting bronchodilator without one is unsafe. Tuberculosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, heart failure, and bronchiectasis are excluded

assessment.display: Exposure to air pollution and indoor solid-fuel smoke
assessment.assessment: Fine particles from coal, wood, and traffic smoke are well-established triggers of asthma symptoms and flares and contribute to lower lung function. Removing indoor solid-fuel smoke is the most effective step within his control; outdoor exposure can be reduced but not removed

recommendations: Diagnosis: asthma with persistent airflow limitation, type 2 phenotype; not COPD. Record the reasoning, and repeat spirometry after three months of treatment to find his best lung function
CT was indicated for persistent airflow limitation in a never-smoker and was done today; it shows airway disease without emphysema or bronchiectasis. No further imaging unless new features appear

Start budesonide-formoterol 160/4.5 mcg, two inhalations twice daily and one as needed, no more than 12 a day (GINA track 1, step 4), and stop albuterol. Teach technique with his own device and give a written action plan. If he is not well controlled at three months despite good adherence and technique, add tiotropium 2.5 mcg two inhalations daily; consider a biologic only if he has flares needing oral corticosteroids despite that
Yes: an eight-week pulmonary rehabilitation program, with a six-minute walk before and after

Keep the open fires out of use permanently and heat his rooms another way; HEPA air cleaners in the rooms where he spends most time; check the air quality index daily and avoid outdoor exertion and city trips when it is 101 or more; a well-fitted N95 respirator on unavoidable alert days; walk away from main roads. The WHO 1687 guideline values for PM2.5 (5 ug/m3 annual, 15 ug/m3 over 24 hours) are a useful target for his indoor monitor

Monitoring: Asthma Control Test, technique, adherence, and exposures at every visit; spirometry and FeNO at three months, then every one to two years; home peak flow to set action-plan zones; influenza, COVID-19, and RSV vaccines in the autumn and PCV20 now
